title: Dysfunktional Family
full_review:
In "Dysfunktional Family" (Miramax), director George Gallo weaves live concert footage with video interviews, creating a raw and raucous portrait of comedian Eddie Griffin. Unfortunately, Griffin's unremitting foul-mouthed rants and lewd tirades detract from his comic wit.

Following in the tradition of Eddie Murphy's "Raw" and "Richard Pryor -- Live in Concert," the film, shot during a recent performance near Griffin's home town of Kansas City, Mo., assaults viewers with an unrelenting barrage of vulgarities in a verbal shock-and-awe campaign. Regrettably, this highly offensive bombardment precludes viewers from considering the occasional astute observation Griffin makes about contemporary American society.

Throughout "Dysfunktional Family," viewers are introduced to various relatives who played a part in molding Griffin and whose support helped him use comedy as a means to escape the dead-end poverty and racism of his youth. Griffin credits his mother, whose legendary tough-love tactics are lampooned throughout, as the stabilizing influence which steered him clear of delinquency and set him on a path to success. He also acknowledges the roles his two colorful uncles played in filling the void left in the absence of his biological father (whom he never met until he was 16 years old).

Griffin's inflammatory shtick seems to be fueled by an ability to find humor in even the most tragic circumstances, including his uncle's battle with addiction, his own anger at being abandoned by his father, and even the dark events of Sept. 11, 2001.

The crass material is uniformly profane and distasteful. The routine caricatures racial groups (including, in all fairness, African-Americans). Organized religion fares no better, with Griffin taking particular delight in unabashedly mocking the Catholic Mass. Viewers must also suffer through crude, misogynistic diatribes intimately detailing his sexual appetites. He defends his seemingly constant use of one particular racial epithet referring to African-Americans by stating that, "The more you say it, the less power it has" to offend.

If any positives can be gleaned, the film does, beneath its abrasive veneer, speak of the importance of family and the positive impact families can have on the lives of their members.

At one point Griffin observes that if God created him to be funny, and if he is created in God's image, then humor and joy in turn must be an integral part of God and his plan for humanity -- which is theologically sound, but one wonders what God would think of his vulgar standup routine?

Due to incessant rough language and profanities, fleeting nudity, sexually explicit references, racial epithets and a pejorative view of religion, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
